claim: Teplizumab delays the onset of clinical type 1 diabetes in at-risk relatives
gold_rationale: Regulatory and clinical consensus supports the claim. The pivotal randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled TrialNet TN-10 trial (Herold et al., NEJM 2019; NCT01030861) in stage 2 (autoantibody-positive, dysglycemic) at-risk relatives showed teplizumab delayed progression to clinical (stage 3) T1D with a hazard ratio of 0.41 (95% CI 0.22-0.78, p=0.006) and a median time-to-diagnosis of 48.4 vs 24.4 months. Extended follow-up (Sims et al., Sci Transl Med 2021, 923-day median) confirmed durability: median 59.6 vs 27.1 months, HR 0.457, p=0.01, with 50% vs 22% remaining diabetes-free. On this single pivotal trial the FDA approved Tzield (teplizumab-mzwv) on 17 Nov 2022 as the first therapy indicated to delay onset of stage 3 T1D in stage 2 patients aged 8+ (expanded to age 1+ on 20 Apr 2026) — a direct regulatory endorsement of the exact claimed effect and population. The claimed outcome (time-to-clinical-diagnosis) is precisely the TN-10 primary endpoint, not a surrogate. The one caveat is that the trial is small (n=76) and single-pivotal, but the effect is statistically robust, replicated in extended follow-up, and regulatorily accepted. The separate PROTECT Phase 3 trial (Ramos, NEJM 2023) addresses a different population/endpoint (C-peptide preservation in already-diagnosed stage 3) and does not bear on the delay-of-onset claim.
outcome: time to clinical (stage 3) type 1 diabetes diagnosis
population: stage 2 T1D (autoantibody-positive, dysglycemic) at-risk relatives of patients with T1D
provenance: Re-verified against PubMed (PMIDs 31180194, 33658358, 37861217, 39608963, 35316839), ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01030861, NCT03875729), and FDA sources (BLA 761183 approval letter, DailyMed TZIELD label, OOPD orphan listing).
notes: All 6 rows verified with no hallucinations. rows.citation: Herold KC, Bundy BN, Long SA, et al. An Anti-CD3 Antibody, Teplizumab, in Relatives at Risk for Type 1 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(7):603-613. DOI:10.1056/NEJMoa1902226 (TrialNet TN-10, NCT01030861).
rows.integrity_note: Verified via PubMed: article types = Randomized Controlled Trial, Clinical Trial Phase II, Multicenter Study, Research Support NIH. Not retracted. NIH/TrialNet funded; basis for FDA approval.
rows.finding: Pivotal Phase 2 double-blind RCT in 76 stage 2 at-risk relatives (44 teplizumab, 32 placebo). Median time to clinical (stage 3) T1D 48.4 vs 24.4 months; HR 0.41 (95% CI 0.22-0.78, p=0.006). Annualized diagnosis rate 14.9% vs 35.9%/yr. Diagnosed in 19/44 (43%) teplizumab vs 23/32 (72%) placebo. Directly supports delay-of-onset on the exact population and clinical endpoint. (Note: FDA label restates the teplizumab-arm count as 20/45%.)

rows.citation: Sims EK, Bundy BN, Stier K, et al. Teplizumab improves and stabilizes beta cell function in antibody-positive high-risk individuals. Sci Transl Med. 2021;13(583):eabc8980. DOI:10.1126/scitranslmed.abc8980.
rows.integrity_note: Verified via PubMed: article types = Randomized Controlled Trial, Research Support NIH. Extended follow-up (923-day median) of the same TN-10 RCT cohort. Not retracted.
rows.finding: Extended follow-up of TN-10 (923-day median). Median time to T1D diagnosis 59.6 vs 27.1 months; HR 0.457 (p=0.01); 50% teplizumab vs 22% placebo remained diabetes-free; also improved on-study C-peptide AUC (1.94 vs 1.72 pmol/ml, p=0.006). Confirms the delay is durable on the clinical endpoint in the claimed population.

rows.citation: Ramos EL, Dayan CM, Chatenoud L, et al. Teplizumab and Beta-Cell Function in Newly Diagnosed Type 1 Diabetes (PROTECT). N Engl J Med. 2023;389(23):2151-2161. DOI:10.1056/NEJMoa2308743 (NCT03875729).
rows.integrity_note: Verified via PubMed: article types = Randomized Controlled Trial, Clinical Trial Phase III. Provention Bio/Sanofi funded. Not retracted. Different population and endpoint from the claim.
rows.finding: Phase 3 RCT in 328 children/adolescents (217 teplizumab, 111 placebo) with NEWLY DIAGNOSED (stage 3) T1D. Primary endpoint was stimulated C-peptide at week 78 (a surrogate for beta-cell function), NOT time to clinical onset. Teplizumab preserved C-peptide (LS-mean diff 0.13 pmol/mL, 95% CI 0.09-0.17, p<0.001); key secondary endpoints not significant. Different population (already diagnosed) and surrogate outcome, so it neither confirms nor refutes the delay-of-onset claim; direction 0 on the claimed outcome.

baseline.text: Yes. Teplizumab (Tzield) delays the onset of clinical, stage 3 type 1 diabetes in at-risk relatives who are at the pre-symptomatic stage 2 (two or more islet autoantibodies plus dysglycemia). The pivotal evidence is the TrialNet TN-10 randomized, placebo-controlled trial (Herold et al., NEJM 2019), in which a single 14-day IV course delayed the median time to clinical T1D from about 24 months on placebo to about 48-50 months on teplizumab, a hazard ratio of ~0.41. Extended follow-up (Sims et al. 2021) showed the effect persisted, with median times to diagnosis of ~60 vs ~27 months. On the strength of this trial the FDA approved teplizumab in November 2022 as the first disease-modifying therapy indicated specifically to delay the onset of stage 3 T1D in stage 2 patients aged 8 and older (later extended to age 1+). So the claim is well supported, though based on a single, relatively small pivotal trial.
